| 15 | **Trunk test** — cover everything but the nav; can you still answer what site / what page / what sections / where am I | design-review Phase 3 | `TOOLS.md` navigation-and-IA section | Checkable rule, and a good one for tool-shaped surfaces where nav debt compounds daily. |
| 16 | **Parallel-worker prompt template** with per-agent retry, quality check, and one-line `VARIANT_x_DONE` / `_FAILED` / `_RATE_LIMITED` report contract | design-shotgun Step 3c | `agents/surface-designer.md`, `agents/technique-prototyper.md` | Operational, but the strict single-line report contract is what makes a fan-out legible to the orchestrator. Also inherit the `/tmp`-then-`cp` workaround. |
| 17 | **Per-mode motion/entry defaults with a stated curve** — `translateY(12px)` + `opacity: 0` over `600ms cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)`, `IntersectionObserver` never `scroll` listener | minimalist-ui §7, high-end-visual-design §5C | `CRAFT.md` motion section | Checkable rule with a named failure ("`window.addEventListener('scroll')` causes continuous reflows and kills mobile performance"). |
| 18 | **Concentric radius rule** — inner radius = outer radius − gap | high-end-visual-design §4A | `CRAFT.md` typographic/surface craft | Checkable rule; two lines; fixes the single most common nested-card tell. |

Deliberately **not** stealing: the Goodwill Reservoir point system, the letter-grade weighted average, the dial-based DESIGN.md config, banned-font lists as a substitute for choosing (see §6).

---

## 6. What they get wrong

**Simulated randomness is not randomness.** `gpt-taste` §1:

> you MUST simulate a Python script execution in your `<design_plan>` before writing any UI code. Use a deterministic seed (e.g., character count of the user prompt modulo math) to simulate `random.choice()`

`high-end-visual-design` §3 does the same thing with dice: "silently 'roll the dice' and select ONE combination." A model asked to simulate an RNG returns its prior with extra steps — and because the prompt is the seed, similar prompts produce identical "rolls." The goal (variance) is correct and is the same goal our `§1`/`§3` hold. The mechanism is theater. Compare `design-shotgun`, which solves the same problem with a test on the *output* rather than a ritual on the input. Lesson for us: enforce distinctness by checking what came out, never by instructing the model to be random.

**Also, count the space.** `high-end-visual-design` promises "NEVER generate the exact same layout or aesthetic twice in a row" over 3 vibes × 3 layouts = 9 outcomes. Nine. Ours is 34 styles × collision × subversion, which is why the collision table has to survive the merge intact.

**Dials that nothing reads.** `stitch-design-taste` opens with four configurable dials, then writes ~120 rules of which exactly two are conditional on a dial ("Centered Hero layouts BANNED when variance exceeds 4"; "When density exceeds 7, all numbers must use Monospace"). Set Creativity to 1 and the file still bans Inter, still bans centered heroes in the shipped `DESIGN.md`, still mandates inline-image-typography as "the signature creative technique." The two files also disagree: `SKILL.md` says centered heroes are banned *above* variance 4, `DESIGN.md` says they are banned flat. A parameter that doesn't change the output is a lie about configurability. If our `TRANSLATE.md` rows do not each visibly change something downstream, we have the same bug — and the spec's own claim that "a blank row is a design decision downstream with no derivation" is the right defense only if we can point at what each row derives.

**Banned-font lists as a proxy for taste.** All six small skills ban Inter. `industrial-brutalist-ui` then recommends it: "**Optimal Web Fonts:** Neue Haas Grotesk (Black), **Inter (Extra Bold/Black)**, Archivo Black..." A direct contradiction inside one skills directory. gstack is more honest — it separates a genuine blacklist (Papyrus, Comic Sans, Lobster) from "overused fonts (never recommend as primary)" and explains the reasoning for Space Grotesk:

> Space Grotesk is on the list specifically because every AI design tool converges on it as "the safe alternative to Inter." That's the convergence trap. Treat it the same as Inter: only use if the user asks for it by name.

That's the correct framing — the ban is about *convergence*, not about the typeface. Our `CRAFT.md`/`STYLES.md` should say the same thing explicitly, or the rule reads as fashion and gets stale in eighteen months.

**Long unordered lists.** `redesign-existing-projects` has ~120 audit items, `stitch-design-taste` 22 anti-patterns, gstack `design-review` "10 categories, ~80 items." Under our bar most individual lines pass as checkable rules. The *sets* mostly fail, because a 120-item list with no order is a backlog. `redesign-existing-projects` redeems itself with Fix Priority. Nothing else does — gstack's design-review checklist runs 80 items and then weights them into a letter grade, which is ordering for *reporting*, not for *acting*.

**Numeric precision that isn't measured.** gstack's Goodwill Reservoir assigns point values (−15 hidden pricing, −10 format punishment, −5 per ambiguous choice), concedes "These scores are heuristic, not measured," and then prints `FINAL: 35/100 ⚠️ CRITICAL UX DEBT`. The underlying observations are excellent; the arithmetic makes them look measured when they are not — which is exactly the failure `devex-review` gets right two skills over with TESTED/INFERRED. Related: `design-review`'s grade computation — "Each category starts at A. Each High-impact finding drops one letter grade" — means five high findings is an F whether they are five typography nits or five failed contrast ratios. Arithmetic wearing judgment's clothes.

**A fix loop with no revert path.** `redesign-existing-projects` scans, diagnoses, and fixes in one uninterrupted pass on someone's working site, with no gate, no verification step, and no rollback. Its Rules say "Do not break existing functionality. Test after every change" and supply neither a test nor a definition of broken. gstack `/design-review`, operating on the same territory, requires a clean working tree up front, commits one fix at a time, re-screenshots, classifies `verified` / `best-effort` / `reverted`, and self-regulates on a risk score with a hard cap of 30 fixes. Whatever we build for redesign inherits gstack's discipline, not the small skill's.

**gstack's own worst problem is duplication.** The 85-line "UX Principles: How Users Actually Behave" block (three laws, satisficing, billboard design, trunk test, goodwill reservoir, mobile) is inlined **verbatim in four skills**: `design-review`, `design-shotgun`, `plan-design-review`, `design-html`. Same for the Design Hard Rules / AI Slop blacklist (three copies) and the Review Readiness Dashboard (three copies). It is generated from templates, so it's cheap to maintain and expensive to read — every design skill pays ~800 lines of preamble plus several hundred lines of duplicated doctrine before reaching its own content. Our 18-file plan must not converge on this. `STYLES.md`, `CRAFT.md`, and `TOOLS.md` are *read on demand* by the loop that needs them; the loops must not inline them. `plan-design-review`'s own Section index pattern is the right answer and gstack already uses it in two places — "This skill is a decision-tree skeleton. The steps below point to on-demand sections. Read a section in full before doing its step; do not work from memory." Copy that mechanism into `AGENTS.md`.

**Nobody covers native.** Our scope claims web + mobile + tablet + desktop. Across all twelve skills, "mobile" means a breakpoint, "tablet" means `768px`, and "desktop" means `1440px`. Not one line addresses iOS, Android, or a desktop application. `imagegen-frontend-mobile` exists elsewhere in the skills directory but is image generation, not design method. The spec's own out-of-scope note — "For iOS or Android the principles hold... and the arsenal does not" — is the right call, and this audit found zero prior art that would let us do better. State the limit in `AGENTS.md` as planned; do not quietly let the four-platform claim in the scope line imply otherwise.

**One more, aimed at us.** Every skill in this corpus that has a "creativity" or "variance" instruction — all six small ones plus `design-consultation`'s anti-convergence directive — is trying to solve the same problem our `§1` states ("creativity is the baseline"). Six of the seven attempts fail because they instruct the model to *be* creative. The one that works (`design-shotgun`'s swap test) checks the artifact. `PRINCIPLES.md §1` is currently an instruction. It needs a check attached, or it joins them.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# inter.face integrity checks. No deps beyond coreutils + jq.
set -uo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." || exit 1
FAIL=0
fail() { printf '  FAIL: %s\n' "$1"; FAIL=1; }
ok()   { printf '  ok: %s\n' "$1"; }

echo "== placeholder scan =="
# The deep-research harness once returned a literal "test claim" / example.com
# stub that passed schema validation. Never let that reach a shipped file.
HITS=$(grep -rniE 'example\.com|\bTBD\b|\bTODO\b|Lorem ipsum|test claim|FIXME|XXX' \
  --include='*.md' --include='*.json' --include='*.mdc' . \
  2>/dev/null | grep -v '^\./docs/' | grep -v '^\./\.git' | grep -v '^\./\.superpowers/' || true)
if [ -n "$HITS" ]; then fail "placeholder text in shipped files:"; echo "$HITS" | sed 's/^/    /'
else ok "no placeholders"; fi

echo "== resident budget =="
if [ -f AGENTS.md ]; then
  N=$(wc -l < AGENTS.md | tr -d ' ')
  [ "$N" -le 200 ] && ok "AGENTS.md ${N} lines (<=200)" || fail "AGENTS.md ${N} lines, budget 200"
else fail "AGENTS.md missing"; fi

echo "== json validity =="
for f in .claude-plugin/plugin.json .claude-plugin/marketplace.json \
         .codex-plugin/plugin.json gemini-extension.json opencode.json; do
  if [ -f "$f" ]; then
    jq empty "$f" 2>/dev/null && ok "$f parses" || fail "$f is not valid JSON"
  else fail "$f missing"; fi
done

echo "== skill frontmatter =="
for f in skills/inter.face/SKILL.md commands/interface.md .cursor/rules/inter.face.mdc; do
  if [ -f "$f" ]; then
    head -1 "$f" | grep -q '^---$' && ok "$f has frontmatter" || fail "$f missing opening ---"
  else fail "$f missing"; fi
done

echo "== internal links resolve =="
BROKEN=0
while IFS= read -r line; do
  src=${line%%:*}; target=${line#*:}
  dir=$(dirname "$src")
  [ -e "$dir/$target" ] || { fail "broken link in $src -> $target"; BROKEN=1; }
done < <(grep -rhoE '\]\(\.{1,2}/[^)#]+\)' --include='*.md' . 2>/dev/null \
         | grep -v '^\./docs/' >/dev/null 2>&1; \
         grep -rnoE '\]\((\.{1,2}/[^)#]+)\)' --include='*.md' . 2>/dev/null \
         | grep -v '/docs/' | grep -v '/\.superpowers/' | sed -E 's/^([^:]+):[0-9]+:\]\((.*)\)$/\1:\2/')
[ "$BROKEN" -eq 0 ] && ok "all relative links resolve"

echo "== every reference file forks on surface class =="
for f in STYLES.md CRAFT.md TOOLS.md SURFACES.md ACCESS.md; do
  if [ -f "$f" ]; then
    if grep -qiE 'page-shaped' "$f" && grep -qiE 'tool-shaped' "$f"; then
      ok "$f forks on surface class"
    else fail "$f does not address both page-shaped and tool-shaped"; fi
  else fail "$f missing"; fi
done

echo "== Apple numbers ship as pairs =="
if [ -f SURFACES.md ]; then
  if grep -qE '(44.*28|28.*44)' SURFACES.md; then
    ok "SURFACES.md carries default AND minimum"
  else fail "SURFACES.md must carry 44pt default AND 28pt minimum, never 44 alone"; fi
else fail "SURFACES.md missing"; fi

echo
[ "$FAIL" -eq 0 ] && echo "ALL CHECKS PASS" || echo "CHECKS FAILED"
exit "$FAIL"

1	# Principles
2	
3	These are the rules that separate a system people run their work on from a demo that
4	impressed everyone in the meeting. Every loop enforces them.
5	
6	Seven of them are **hard** (`§7`, `§8`, `§10`, `§12`, `§14`, `§18`, `§22`) — they
7	cannot be skipped, waived, or traded away, because they are about data people cannot
8	get back, access people should not have, and going live under someone else's name. They
9	are marked **[HARD]**. Everything else is skippable by the human, at a stated cost
10	(see [`SKIPPING.md`](./SKIPPING.md)).
11	
12	A website is read. **A system is operated.** Somebody sits in front of this for seven
13	hours a day, their work is inside it, and when it is wrong they cannot go elsewhere.
14	That difference drives every rule below.
15	
16	---
17	
18	## 0. Intake before anything. Map the process that exists, not the one they describe.
19	
20	Before you model, design, or build, watch the work happen. What people say they do and
21	what they do are different, and the gap is where every requirements document goes
22	wrong.
23	
24	- **The process today**, step by step, including the spreadsheet, the WhatsApp group,
25	  and the printed form somebody still fills in. Those are not workarounds to eliminate;
26	  they are requirements nobody wrote down.
27	- **The exceptions.** Ask what happens when it goes wrong, when a customer is
28	  difficult, when the number does not match. Systems die on exceptions, and the
29	  happy path is the easy half.
30	- **The numbers.** Records per day, users, peak, growth, the biggest table, the longest
31	  report.
32	- **What must not change.** A legally required document number, a code the accountant
33	  needs, an export the bank expects.
34	- **Explicit do-nots.** Honor absolutely.
35	
36	Ask open-ended, one at a time. Ask to see it rather than to be told about it. If you
37	can, sit with someone doing the job for an hour — that hour is worth a week of
38	specification.
39	
40	## 1. Name the one decision-maker, and the one operator.
41	
42	Two people, and they are rarely the same person.
43	
44	**The decision-maker** approves scope, budget, and every gate. One name, in writing, at
45	Gate A. Everyone else's input is input.
46	
47	**The operator** is whoever will actually use this all day. They are usually not in the
48	room, they are usually not senior, and they are the only person who can tell you
49	whether a screen works. Get one named operator you can show things to, and show them
50	early. A system signed off by management and hated by the people using it is the normal
51	failure of this category.
52	
53	## 2. Scope is the product. The kill list is a deliverable.
54	
55	Every system project fails the same way: it grows until it cannot ship. The defense is
56	written, agreed, and visible.
57	
58	At Gate A you produce two lists. **In v1**, which is short. And **not in v1**, which is
59	long, specific, and signed — not "later" as a feeling, but a named list of things that
60	are deliberately absent, so that the fourth request in month two meets a document
61	rather than a shrug.
62	
63	The kill list is not a rejection of the ideas on it. It is the reason the things above
64	it ship.
65	
66	## 3. Model the domain in their words. The schema is the contract.
67	
68	Entities get the names the business already uses. If they say "job" do not call it a
69	`WorkOrder`, and if they distinguish a "quote" from an "estimate", find out why before
70	merging them — that distinction is usually load-bearing.
71	
72	The data model is the one decision that is expensive to change later. Everything else
73	is code you can rewrite. Get the entities, the relationships, the invariants, the state
74	machines, and the identifiers right at Loop 2, and write down what makes each record
75	valid. See [`DOMAIN.md`](./DOMAIN.md).
76	
77	## 4. Ship vertical slices to production, not layers.
78	
79	Never "build the whole schema, then the whole API, then the whole UI." Build one
80	complete path — schema, migration, endpoint, authorization, interface, tests, seed
81	data — and put it in front of the operator.
82	
83	A slice that a real person can complete a real task with is worth more than three
84	layers that are each 80% done, because it is the only thing that produces the feedback
85	the next slice needs. See [`SCOPE.md`](./SCOPE.md).
86	
87	## 5. The architecture is boring on purpose.
88	
89	One database, one deployable, one language, the framework's defaults. A monolith with
90	clear internal boundaries beats six services for every system this pipeline is likely
91	to build, and it beats them on the exact dimension that matters: how fast a change can
92	be made safely a year from now, by somebody else.
93	
94	Every deviation from boring is an argument you have to make at Gate B, in writing, with
95	the operational cost stated. "We might need to scale" is not that argument.
96	
97	Choose what the client's team can maintain. A stack nobody there can hire for is a
98	dependency dressed as a decision. See [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](./ARCHITECTURE.md).
99	
100	## 6. The interface is not boring, and it is designed for the operator's day.
101	
102	`§5` buys you the budget to spend here. A system's interface is used for hours, not
103	seconds, which inverts every rule a marketing site follows: density is a feature,
104	keyboard paths beat clicks, and the third-most-common action still needs to be two
105	keystrokes away.
106	
107	Design the **day**, not the screen. What do they do forty times before lunch? That
108	sequence gets the design attention, and the settings page nobody opens does not. Reject
109	the generic admin template — an operator can tell within a minute whether anyone
110	thought about their job. See [`INTERFACE.md`](./INTERFACE.md).
111	
112	---
113	
114	## 7. Authorization is proven by a test on every path. **[HARD]**
115	
116	Not "we added a permission check". A test, per endpoint and per action, that asserts
117	the wrong role is **denied** — and that fails if someone removes the check.
118	
119	Authentication is who you are; authorization is what you may touch, and it is the one
120	that leaks. The common failure is not a missing login screen, it is an endpoint that
121	checks the user is signed in and never checks the record belongs to them. That bug is
122	invisible in the UI, because the UI never shows the button.
123	
124	Every new endpoint ships with its denial test in the same commit. No exceptions for
125	internal tools — "internal" means the blast radius is employees' data instead of
126	customers'. See [`SECURITY.md`](./SECURITY.md).
127	
128	## 8. Isolation is proven, not assumed. **[HARD]**
129	
130	If the system serves more than one company, branch, or customer, prove that one cannot
131	read another's data. A test that creates two tenants, writes to both, and asserts each
132	sees only its own — on every listing, every detail view, every export, every report,
133	every search, and every file download.
134	
135	The leak is almost never on the main list view somebody tested. It is in the CSV
136	export, the print view, the notification email, the autocomplete, or the audit log.
137	
138	Enforce it at the lowest layer you can, ideally in the database, so a forgotten `WHERE`
139	clause fails closed rather than open.
140	
141	## 9. Every state is designed.
142	
143	Nine of them, and the first one is the one people ship without: **empty**, loading,
144	partial, error, **permission-denied**, offline or degraded, stale, conflicting, and
145	bulk.
146	
147	A new system's first screen is always empty, and an empty state that says "No records"
148	teaches nobody what to do. A permission-denied state that looks like a crash generates
149	a support ticket every time. A conflict state that silently overwrites somebody's
150	edit destroys work, and they will not know.
151	
152	If it is not designed, it will be discovered by the operator on a bad day.
153	
154	## 10. Data loss is unrecoverable. **[HARD]**
155	
156	Three commitments, all of them tested rather than intended:
157	
158	- **Every migration is reversible**, or it is preceded by a backup taken and verified
159	  in the same run. A destructive migration with no down path does not deploy.
160	- **Restore is drilled before go-live.** A backup you have never restored is not a
161	  backup, it is a file. Restore into a scratch environment, run the smoke tests
162	  against it, and record how long it took. That number is the client's real recovery
163	  time.
164	- **Deletion is soft by default**, with a real deletion path that is deliberate and
165	  logged. An operator will delete the wrong thing in week one.
166	
167	See [`DATA.md`](./DATA.md).
168	
169	## 11. Correctness before throughput.
170	
171	Money, stock, hours, and anything a regulator counts get exact arithmetic — integer
172	minor units or fixed-point decimals, never floats. Rounding is defined once, in one
173	place, and matches what the accountant does.
174	
175	Anything that can be submitted twice is idempotent: a payment, an order, a webhook, a
176	stock movement, a report generation. Assume every request will arrive twice, because
177	the network, the user's double-click, and the partner's retry policy all guarantee it.
178	
179	Where a rule about money and a rule about performance conflict, money wins, and the
180	performance problem is solved another way.
181	
182	## 12. Secrets, personal data, and the audit trail. **[HARD]**
183	
184	**Secrets** never enter the repository, the logs, the error tracker, or a screenshot.
185	They live in the environment or a secret store, on the client's account, and there is a
186	documented way to rotate each one.
187	
188	**Personal data** is known: what is stored, why, on what basis, for how long, and how it
189	gets deleted when someone asks. A system that cannot answer those five questions cannot
190	be operated lawfully in most of the markets this pipeline builds for. Do not log it,
191	do not put it in an analytics event, and do not copy production data into staging
192	without masking it (`DATA.md`).
193	
194	**The audit trail** records who did what to which record and when, for anything
195	financial, personal, or permission-related. It is append-only, it is not editable by
196	the application, and it is the first thing anyone asks for after an incident.
197	
198	## 13. Observability ships with the feature, not after the incident.
199	
200	Every slice arrives with structured logs carrying a request id, an error report that
201	reaches a human, and one metric that would show this feature failing. A background job
202	gets an alert for "has not run" as well as for "crashed" — silent jobs are the failure
203	nobody notices for a month.
204	
205	The test: if this breaks at 3am, what does the person on call see, and is it enough?
206	See [`OPERATE.md`](./OPERATE.md).
207	
208	## 14. Accessible and keyboard-complete. **[HARD]**
209	
210	Someone uses this all day, every day, and some of them use a screen reader, or cannot
211	use a mouse, or have been doing this job for eleven years and can type faster than any
212	pointer.
213	
214	Semantic HTML, real labels on every field, errors announced and associated, visible
215	focus, contrast at 4.5:1, and **every primary workflow completable by keyboard alone**.
216	Tables with real headers. Modals that trap and return focus. Nothing conveyed by color
217	alone, because your status column will be read by someone who cannot see the
218	difference between your green and your red.
219	
220	This is hard for the ordinary reason — it locks real people out of their own job — and
221	for the legal one, since an employment tool that cannot be operated by a disabled
222	employee is a problem in most jurisdictions.
223	
224	## 15. Performance is a workflow constraint. Measure the operator's task.
225	
226	The p95 of an endpoint is not the number that matters. The number that matters is how
227	long the operator's most repeated task takes, end to end, on the hardware and the
228	network they actually have — which for a warehouse is a five-year-old Android on
229	patchy wifi, and for a back office is a browser with forty tabs open.
230	
231	Budget it in Loop 2, measure it in Loop 4 against realistic data volume, and remember
232	that the table with 40 rows in development has 4 million in production. A list view
233	that was fast on seed data is the most common performance surprise there is.
234	
235	## 16. Integrations fail. Design for their bad day.
236	
237	Every external system will be down, slow, rate-limited, or wrong. Assume it, and never
238	let it take the core workflow with it.
239	
240	Retries with backoff, idempotency keys, a dead-letter path someone can see, timeouts on
241	everything, and reconciliation — a way to answer "are we in sync?" without trusting
242	that every message arrived. A queue that silently drops is worse than an integration
243	that visibly fails.
244	
245	Where a partner's outage would block the operator, design the manual path they use
246	until it comes back.
247	
248	## 17. Migration from the old system is the hardest half.
249	
250	It is also the half that gets a line in the plan and a week at the end. Legacy data is
251	inconsistent, incomplete, and full of conventions nobody documented — a status column
252	with nine values, three of which mean the same thing, and one that means "Jan left".

256	it is boring, and plan the cutover with the client's calendar in front of you. See

258

262	they were told about, not a feature flag switched at 80%, not "we soft-launched to a
263	few people".
264	
265	The other gates — A (domain and scope), B (architecture and contracts), C (experience),
266	D (per slice) — can be collapsed on request, at a cost recorded in `SKIPS.md`. Gate E
267	cannot, because on the other side of it are real people's real work and real data.
268	
269	## 19. Test what breaking would cost.
270	
271	Not a coverage number. A judgment about consequence, and it produces a short list of
272	tests that must exist and always pass:
273	
274	- Every authorization path (`§7`) and every isolation boundary (`§8`)

276	- Every state machine's illegal transitions, asserted as rejected
277	- Every migration, forward and backward, on production-shaped data
278	- The one end-to-end path that is the reason the system exists
279	
280	Everything else is worth testing in proportion to how often it changes and how loudly
281	it fails. See [`QUALITY.md`](./QUALITY.md).
282	
283	## 20. Environments are real, and staging looks like production.
284	
285	Local, staging, production. Staging runs the same migrations, the same configuration
286	shape, and **production-shaped data** — the same volume and the same messiness, with
287	personal data masked (`§12`).
288	
289	Staging with 40 clean rows proves nothing. Most of what goes wrong in production is a
290	data shape nobody had locally.
291	
292	## 21. Documentation is a runbook and an operator guide.
293	
294	Two documents, both short, both tested by someone following them.
295	
296	**The runbook** is for whoever is on call: how to deploy, how to roll back, how to
297	restore, what each alert means, who to call, and the three things that have gone wrong
298	before.
299	
300	**The operator guide** is for the person doing the job: how to do the five most common
301	tasks, what the statuses mean, and what to do when it says no.
302	
303	An architecture diagram nobody reads is not documentation. A README that tells a new
304	developer how to get the system running in one command is.
305	
306	## 22. Push and deploy as them. **[HARD]**
307	
308	This pipeline writes commits, pushes to a real repository, and deploys under a real
309	company's name to infrastructure holding real data. Getting the identity wrong puts
310	your name on their system, or theirs on yours, and puts their production credentials in
311	your session.
312	
313	Use **their** authenticated identity throughout. Git config set inside the run's repo,
314	never globally. Their cloud account, their database, their secret store, so they can
315	revoke, redeploy, and move without you. Verify before the first push and again before
316	every production deploy, and read the output:
317	
318	```bash
319	git -C <repo> config user.email       # theirs, not yours
320	gh auth status                         # their login, the right host
321	<cloud> whoami / sts get-caller-identity
322	echo "$DATABASE_URL" | sed 's/:.*@/:***@/'   # which database am I actually pointed at
323	```
324	
325	That last one has saved more data than every other check on this list. A mismatch stops
326	the run until the human resolves it.
327	
328	## 23. Skipping is allowed, silent degradation is not.
329	
330	The human may skip any non-**[HARD]** step. When they do: record it in
331	`runs/<slug>/SKIPS.md` with what that step would have caught, carry it into the final
332	confidence grade, and do not raise it again. State the cost once, accept the answer,
333	keep moving.
334	
335	Never skip a step on your own initiative to save time, and never skip a hard rule
336	because the deadline is real. The deadline is always real.
337	
338	## 24. Match the model tier to the cost of being wrong.
339	
340	A step whose mistake the next command catches is cheap to get wrong. A step whose
341	output every later loop consumes is not.
342	
343	The process mapping, the domain model, the scope call, the architecture decision, and
344	every gate are top tier — a wrong entity name is a rename, a wrong relationship is a
345	rewrite. Scaffolding, mechanical migration, and checklist verification are not.
346	Dispatch workers at the tier the work needs ([`MODELS.md`](./MODELS.md)) without
347	asking.
348	
349	## 25. The system's own words are written, not generated.
350	
351	Every label, status, empty state, confirmation, and error message is deliberate copy in
352	the operator's vocabulary, and it uses the client's nouns from `§3`.
353	
354	Especially the errors. "Something went wrong" is an unwritten string, and in a system it
355	is worse than on a website: the operator cannot leave and try a competitor, they have to
356	file a ticket and wait. Say what happened, whether their work was saved, and what to do
357	next.
358	
359	No slop: no "seamless", no "powerful", no exclamation marks in a status column, and no
360	cheerful copy in front of a failed payment.
361	
362	## 26. Attribution is on by default — visible, and always removable.
363	
364	Every system this pipeline builds carries a small **"Built with systemcicy"** line in
365	its About or admin footer, linking to the repo and to
366	[PIIIX](https://github.com/PIIIX-org), plus the marker comment
367	`<!-- forged-with: systemcicy -->`.
368	
369	It stays visible rather than hidden, and the human can delete it by hand — tell them it
370	is there, that removing it is fine, and never re-add it after they have.
371

impressed everyone in the meeting. Every loop enforces them.

Seven of them are **hard** (`§7`, `§8`, `§10`, `§12`, `§14`, `§18`, `§22`) — they
cannot be skipped, waived, or traded away, because they are about data people cannot
get back, access people should not have, and going live under someone else's name. They
are marked **[HARD]**. Everything else is skippable by the human, at a stated cost
(see [`SKIPPING.md`](./SKIPPING.md)).

A website is read. **A system is operated.** Somebody sits in front of this for seven
hours a day, their work is inside it, and when it is wrong they cannot go elsewhere.
That difference drives every rule below.

---

## 0. Intake before anything. Map the process that exists, not the one they describe.

Before you model, design, or build, watch the work happen. What people say they do and
what they do are different, and the gap is where every requirements document goes
wrong.

- **The process today**, step by step, including the spreadsheet, the WhatsApp group,
  and the printed form somebody still fills in. Those are not workarounds to eliminate;
  they are requirements nobody wrote down.
- **The exceptions.** Ask what happens when it goes wrong, when a customer is
  difficult, when the number does not match. Systems die on exceptions, and the
  happy path is the easy half.
- **The numbers.** Records per day, users, peak, growth, the biggest table, the longest
  report.
- **What must not change.** A legally required document number, a code the accountant
  needs, an export the bank expects.
- **Explicit do-nots.** Honor absolutely.

Ask open-ended, one at a time. Ask to see it rather than to be told about it. If you
can, sit with someone doing the job for an hour — that hour is worth a week of
specification.

## 1. Name the one decision-maker, and the one operator.

**The decision-maker** approves scope, budget, and every gate. One name, in writing, at
Gate A. Everyone else's input is input.

**The operator** is whoever will actually use this all day. They are usually not in the
room, they are usually not senior, and they are the only person who can tell you
whether a screen works. Get one named operator you can show things to, and show them
early. A system signed off by management and hated by the people using it is the normal
failure of this category.

Local, staging, production. Staging runs the same migrations, the same configuration
shape, and **production-shaped data** — the same volume and the same messiness, with
personal data masked (`§12`).

Staging with 40 clean rows proves nothing. Most of what goes wrong in production is a
data shape nobody had locally.

## 21. Documentation is a runbook and an operator guide.

Two documents, both short, both tested by someone following them.

**The runbook** is for whoever is on call: how to deploy, how to roll back, how to
restore, what each alert means, who to call, and the three things that have gone wrong
before.

**The operator guide** is for the person doing the job: how to do the five most common
tasks, what the statuses mean, and what to do when it says no.

An architecture diagram nobody reads is not documentation. A README that tells a new
developer how to get the system running in one command is.

## 22. Push and deploy as them. **[HARD]**

This pipeline writes commits, pushes to a real repository, and deploys under a real
company's name to infrastructure holding real data. Getting the identity wrong puts
your name on their system, or theirs on yours, and puts their production credentials in
your session.

Use **their** authenticated identity throughout. Git config set inside the run's repo,
never globally. Their cloud account, their database, their secret store, so they can
revoke, redeploy, and move without you. Verify before the first push and again before
every production deploy, and read the output:

```bash
git -C <repo> config user.email       # theirs, not yours
gh auth status                         # their login, the right host
<cloud> whoami / sts get-caller-identity
echo "$DATABASE_URL" | sed 's/:.*@/:***@/'   # which database am I actually pointed at
```

That last one has saved more data than every other check on this list. A mismatch stops
the run until the human resolves it.

## 23. Skipping is allowed, silent degradation is not.

The human may skip any non-**[HARD]** step. When they do: record it in
`runs/<slug>/SKIPS.md` with what that step would have caught, carry it into the final
confidence grade, and do not raise it again. State the cost once, accept the answer,
keep moving.

Never skip a step on your own initiative to save time, and never skip a hard rule
because the deadline is real. The deadline is always real.

## 24. Match the model tier to the cost of being wrong.

A step whose mistake the next command catches is cheap to get wrong. A step whose
output every later loop consumes is not.

The process mapping, the domain model, the scope call, the architecture decision, and
every gate are top tier — a wrong entity name is a rename, a wrong relationship is a
rewrite. Scaffolding, mechanical migration, and checklist verification are not.
Dispatch workers at the tier the work needs ([`MODELS.md`](./MODELS.md)) without
asking.

## 25. The system's own words are written, not generated.

Every label, status, empty state, confirmation, and error message is deliberate copy in
the operator's vocabulary, and it uses the client's nouns from `§3`.

Especially the errors. "Something went wrong" is an unwritten string, and in a system it
is worse than on a website: the operator cannot leave and try a competitor, they have to
file a ticket and wait. Say what happened, whether their work was saved, and what to do
next.

No slop: no "seamless", no "powerful", no exclamation marks in a status column, and no
cheerful copy in front of a failed payment.

## 26. Attribution is on by default — visible, and always removable.

Every system this pipeline builds carries a small **"Built with systemcicy"** line in
its About or admin footer, linking to the repo and to
[PIIIX](https://github.com/PIIIX-org), plus the marker comment
`<!-- forged-with: systemcicy -->`.

It stays visible rather than hidden, and the human can delete it by hand — tell them it
is there, that removing it is fine, and never re-add it after they have.

# inter.face Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Build the inter.face plugin — a cross-agent, design-only pipeline that takes a six-row translation table and produces `DIRECTION.md`, `tokens.json`, one design image per surface, and one measured prototype per technique.

**Architecture:** Plain markdown, no runtime. A thin always-resident router (`AGENTS.md`) routes to on-demand reference files. Seven per-agent adapter files all point at that one router. Content is merged from three parent repos plus 10 verified research documents. A shell check script is the test harness.

**Tech Stack:** Markdown, JSON, one bash check script (`jq`, `grep`, `awk` — no dependencies to install).

## Global Constraints

- **Sourcing rule (HARD).** No quotation ships unless it was read off a rendered primary source and is recorded in `docs/research/`. Three fabricated quotes were caught during research; two summarizer fabrications in the WCAG run, one Liquid Glass stacking rule attributed to a page that does not contain it. Any quote whose text cannot be found in `docs/research/*.md` fails `scripts/check.sh`.
- **No placeholder leakage (HARD).** A research workflow returned a literal `"test claim"` sourced to `example.com` that passed schema validation. `scripts/check.sh` greps for `example.com`, `TBD`, `TODO`, `Lorem`, `test claim`, `FIXME` across all shipped markdown. Zero tolerance.
- **Resident budget.** `AGENTS.md` ≤ 200 lines. It is the only always-loaded file.
- **Every reference file opens with its page-shaped and tool-shaped answer**, before any other content. Forking only the loop body was v1's error.
- **No subject-indexed catalogs.** Keying guidance on "what should a *funeral home* look like" is the category reflex mechanized. Key on visual family, surface class, or measurable property only.
- **Attribution.** README credits `portfolio.me`, `webcrab`, `systemcicy` as parents.
- **Identity.** All commits as `Taha-Mahmoodi <85902429+Taha-Mahmoodi@users.noreply.github.com>`. The repo already has this in local git config. Never let the `sadeqisaidmohaddes-star` gh account become active during this work.
- **Apple numbers ship as pairs.** Never "44pt minimum" — always default *and* minimum, per platform. This was the single most-repeated error found in the competitive landscape.

## File Structure

| File | Responsibility | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENTS.md` | Universal entry, routing table, scope + limits. Always resident. | New |
| `PRINCIPLES.md` | 16 rules, 3 hard | portfolio.me `PRINCIPLES.md` subset + systemcicy |
| `TRANSLATE.md` | The 6-row input contract | New, from BRAND/POSITIONING convergence |
| `STYLES.md` | What it looks like: families, picking, clichés, collision, density | pf.me + webcrab merge |
| `CRAFT.md` | How it renders: arsenal, prototypes, budget, motion, **icons** | pf.me + webcrab merge |
| `TOOLS.md` | Tool-shaped surfaces: 9 states, density, keyboard, forms, tables | systemcicy `INTERFACE.md` |
| `SURFACES.md` | Mobile / tablet / desktop platform law + numbers | Research docs |
| `ACCESS.md` | Accessibility as Loop-1 decisions, **+ i18n** | Research docs |
| `REDESIGN.md` | Brownfield: correction vs reposition fork | Audit findings |
| `BREAKING.md` | When to break a rule deliberately | Authored |
| `loops/01-direction.md` | Palette, type, concepts, images → Gate A | pf.me loop 2a + steals |
| `loops/02-craft.md` | Technique, prototypes, motion, budget → Gate B | pf.me loop 2b + steals |

depending on the surface class.

# Tools

Designing for the operator's day.

`STYLES.md` is what an interface looks like; `CRAFT.md` is how you render it. This file is
what it must **do** when it is used for hours, every day, by the same person — the one
place in the plugin where **tool-shaped** is not a fork, it is the whole subject.

Read row 1 of `TRANSLATE.md` first. If it reads **page-shaped** — read for seconds, once —
this file has nothing to add past what `STYLES.md` and `CRAFT.md` already carry: stop here.
If it reads **tool-shaped** — read for hours, daily — everything below is for you, and it
is the only file in the plugin that is.

`§11` buys the budget; `§15` spends it here. A system's interface is used for hours, not
seconds, which inverts nearly every rule a marketing site follows: density is a feature,
keyboard beats pointer, and delight is measured in keystrokes removed rather than in
animation.

The generic admin template is the failure mode. An operator can tell inside a minute
whether anyone thought about their job.

---

## 1. Design the day, not the screen

Before any screen, write the operator's day as a sequence with counts:

> Opens the queue at 08:00. 40 new jobs. Assigns each to a technician — reads the
> address, checks who is nearest, drags or types a name. Two minutes each, interrupted
> constantly by the phone. At 11:00, three jobs come back rejected and have to be
> re-scheduled. At 16:30 she runs the day's completion report and emails it.

That paragraph decides everything. Assignment happens 40 times, so it gets the design
attention and it does not open a modal. The report happens once, so it can be plain.
"Interrupted constantly" means the screen must survive being left and returned to, which
means state in the URL and no unsaved work in a modal.

Do this per role. Three days written out are worth more than twenty wireframes.

### The three questions to ask the operator

At Gate A, and again at Gate B:

1. What do you do most often?
2. What takes the longest and shouldn't?
3. What do you do when it goes wrong?

The third finds the states nobody designs (below).

## 2. Density is a feature

An operator wants to see forty rows, not six cards with generous whitespace. A marketing
site's spacing scale applied to an operations table is actively hostile: it turns one
screen of work into six scrolls.

- Tight, consistent row heights with a comfortable option for people who need it
- Real tables for tabular data — semantic, sortable, with sticky headers
- Numbers right-aligned and tabular-figure aligned so columns compare at a glance
- Truncation with the full value available, never a layout that reflows on content
- Column choice belongs to the operator: which columns, what width, what order,
  remembered

Density is not clutter. Clutter is undifferentiated density — everything the same
weight. Hierarchy is what makes forty rows readable.

## 3. Keyboard completeness (`§15`, hard)

Every primary workflow completable by keyboard alone. Not as an accessibility checkbox —
though it is that — but because the person who has done this job for eleven years types
faster than any pointer.

- Tab order follows the visual order, and focus is always visible
- The primary action of a form is `Enter`; the escape from anything is `Escape`
- A command palette or a "go to" shortcut once the system has more than a handful of
  screens
- Shortcuts for the top three actions of each screen, discoverable rather than secret —
  a `?` overlay, and hints on the buttons themselves
- Search focusable with one key from anywhere
- In a table: arrow keys move, `Enter` opens, `Space` selects, `Shift` extends
- Never trap focus except in a modal, and a modal always returns focus where it came
  from

Watch a fast operator use the old system. If they are using keyboard shortcuts there and
your version does not have them, you have made their day slower and no feature list will
compensate.

## 4. The nine states

Every view, every time. Designed, not defaulted.

| State | What it must do | The failure |
|---|---|---|
| **Empty** | Teach what this is and offer the first action | "No records found" on a brand-new system, so nobody knows what to do |
| **Loading** | Preserve layout. Skeletons over spinners on anything structured | Content jumping when it arrives |
| **Partial** | Show what loaded, name what did not | One failing widget blanking the page |
| **Error** | What happened, whether their work was saved, what to do next | "Something went wrong" |
| **Permission denied** | A designed state explaining who can do this, not a crash | Looks like a bug, generates a ticket every time |
| **Offline / degraded** | Say what still works, queue what can be queued | Silent failures that look like success |
| **Stale** | Say when data was fetched, offer refresh | Somebody acting on a number from twenty minutes ago |
| **Conflict** | Somebody else changed this. Show both, let the human choose | **Silently overwriting somebody's work**, which they will never know about |
| **Bulk** | Progress, partial success, and what failed and why | "12 of 400 failed" with no list |

The empty state is the first thing every user sees on a new system and it is the most
neglected. The conflict state is the one that destroys work.

### Desktop window states

A different axis from the nine above — those answer what the data is doing; this answers
what the window is doing, and it only exists on a desktop-shaped surface. A web page has
no concept of being visible but not focused, with a different chrome treatment; a desktop
window does, and a desktop-shaped tool is designed against three of them, not one:

| State | What it must do | The failure |
|---|---|---|
| **Main** | The window someone is working in. Content and controls read as fully live | Treating "not the frontmost app" the same as "not receiving input," which erases a state the operator actually relies on |
| **Key** | Receives keyboard input right now. Window controls (close, minimize, zoom) render in color; a window becomes key only when someone clicks its title bar or a component that requires keyboard input | A custom title bar that never changes, so an operator with several windows open cannot tell which one their next keystroke lands in |
| **Inactive** | Window chrome — including those same controls — grays out, signaling "not receiving input" without hiding content | Content that dims or disables along with the chrome, so a background window an operator is monitoring goes unreadable |

If the window is custom-chromed rather than system-default, these three states have to be
hand-implemented — the system does not update a custom title bar's appearance for you.
Window controls sit at the leading edge of the toolbar, and critical information or
actions never sit where that chrome can cover them.

## 5. Forms

Where an operator spends most of the day.

- **Label above the field.** Always visible, never placeholder-only
- Group by the mental model of the task, not by the table's columns
- Sensible defaults, and remember the last value where the same value repeats
- Required marked, and optional marked too when most fields are required
- Validate on blur, not per keystroke. Errors next to the field, in words, announced
- **Never lose what they typed.** Not on validation error, not on session expiry, not on
  a failed save. This is the fastest way to lose an operator's trust and it is
  unforgivable when their input took four minutes
- Autosave on long forms, with visible state, or a warning before leaving
- `Enter` submits; the primary button says what it does — "Create order", not "Save"
- Inline creation for the referenced thing that does not exist yet. Making someone
  abandon a form to create a customer, then start again, is a design failure that costs
  minutes forty times a day
- Big number entry gets the right keyboard and the right input mode on mobile
- Duplicate detection before submission where duplicates matter, not a unique-constraint
  error afterward

## 6. Tables and lists

- Filter, sort, and search state **in the URL**, so it can be bookmarked, shared with a
  colleague, and survives a reload — this is the single highest-value detail in an
  operations interface
- Pagination that survives inserts (cursor-based) on anything long
- Row actions reachable without a hover-only menu; hover-only is unusable by touch and
  by keyboard
- Bulk selection with a real count, a select-all-matching option distinct from
  select-all-on-page, and a confirmation that names what will happen to how many
- Saved views per operator for the filters they use every day
- Export from the current filtered view, not the whole table, and say which it is
- Empty-after-filter is a different state from empty-overall, with a different message
  and a clear-filters action

## 7. Navigation and information architecture

- Structured by the operator's tasks, not by the database schema. "Today's jobs" is a
  navigation item; `job_assignments` is not
- The five most-used destinations reachable in one action from anywhere
- Current location always obvious, and deep pages breadcrumbed
- Search that spans entities and understands identifiers — pasting an order number
  should find the order
- Role-shaped navigation: an operator does not see admin sections they cannot use, and
  hiding is in addition to the server-side check, never instead of it

**The trunk test**, from gstack's design-review: cover everything but the navigation
chrome and look at what's left. Can you still answer what site or system this is, what
page you're on, what sections exist, and where you are inside them? If blocking out the
nav erases the answer, the content and hierarchy were leaning on the chrome to do work
they should be doing themselves — and a tool-shaped surface pays for that gap every day,
not once, the way a page-shaped visitor who bounces after one confused look does not.

## 8. Feedback, confirmation, and undo

- Every action produces visible feedback within 100ms, even if only optimistic
- **Undo beats confirm.** A confirmation dialog is trained away in a week and clicked
  through; an undo works even after the mistake. Use undo for anything reversible
- Confirm only what cannot be undone, and make the dialog state the consequence
  specifically: "Delete 34 orders. This cannot be undone."
- Destructive actions are visually distinct and never the default focus
- Long operations run in the background with progress and a notification, not a frozen
  screen

## 9. The system's words

Labels, statuses, empty states, confirmations, and errors are deliberate copy in the
operator's vocabulary, using the operator's own nouns for their own concepts.

Errors especially. In a system the operator cannot go elsewhere; they file a ticket and
wait. Say what happened, whether their work was saved, and what to do next:

> **Couldn't save this order.** The customer's credit limit was reduced while you were
> editing. Your changes are still here — reduce the total to £4,200 or ask a manager to
> override.

No "Something went wrong". No exclamation marks in a status column. No cheerful copy in
front of a failed payment.

## 10. Mobile and field use

If any role works away from a desk, that is a different design, not a narrower one.

- Large touch targets, thumb-reachable primary actions, and no hover dependency
- Works in sunlight: contrast well above the minimum
- Works with gloves, in a warehouse, on a five-year-old Android with two bars
- Offline behavior explicit if it was decided at Gate B: what queues, what does not,
  what the conflict state is
- Camera, scanner, and signature where the work uses them
- Never require a desktop step in the middle of a field workflow

## 11. Performance as felt (`§11`)

The number that matters is the operator's task time, not the endpoint's p95.

- Optimistic UI for anything that almost always succeeds, with a real reconcile on
  failure
- Perceived speed: instant feedback, skeletons that match the final layout, prefetch on
  intent
- Test every list view against realistic volume. The table with 40 rows in development
  has 4 million in production, and the list view that was fast on seed data is the most
  common performance surprise there is
- No layout shift after load. An operator clicking where a button was is a real error
  with real consequences

## 12. The design system

Small and strict. Tokens for color, space, type, radius, and motion; one component per
job; every component with all its states designed — default, hover, focus-visible,
active, disabled, error, and loading.

Two things a system needs that a marketing site does not: a **status vocabulary** (a
fixed set of statuses with fixed colors *and* shapes or labels, never color alone
(`§10`)), and a **data display set** — currency, quantity, date, relative time, person,
identifier — each formatted one way everywhere, from one component.

None of this prescribes a look. "Small and strict" constrains the token set, not the
style — `STYLES.md`'s picking procedure applies here exactly as it does page-shaped, and
a tool-shaped surface earns a deliberate style the same as any other: chosen at Gate A,
checked against style-under-density before it is trusted with forty rows. The plainest
possible system is a choice like every other in `STYLES.md`, not the default a tool is
owed — the generic admin template is what happens when nobody makes it.

Dark mode is worth it for anyone working long hours or at night. Design it, do not
invert it.

## 13. The deliverable

For a tool-shaped surface, `DIRECTION.md` carries these nine things in addition to
whatever `loops/02-craft.md` already requires it to hit at rendered-style resolution,
decided across Gate A and Gate B:

1. **The day, per role** — the sequences with counts
2. **The screen inventory** and which task each serves
3. **Key flows** — designed, with all nine states per screen
4. **Keyboard map** — shortcuts per screen and the global ones
5. **The design system** — tokens, components, status vocabulary, data formats
6. **Density decisions** — row heights, table defaults, what is configurable
7. **Mobile and field** design if applicable
8. **Copy** — labels, statuses, empty states, error messages
9. **Accessibility notes** — focus order, announcements, anything unusual

## Skip cost

Skipping this — designing the operator's day rather than the screen — still produces a
working system with a generic admin interface. It passes every test, and the operator is
slower than they were with the spreadsheet. That is the most common way a technically
successful system fails, and it is discovered after go-live when the sunk cost makes it
hardest to fix.

# Task 6 report — TOOLS.md

**Branch:** `build/plugin-files`
**Commit:** `bb22df63cbe5be1e9f78e21627553bb7252a4b94`
**File shipped:** `TOOLS.md` (273 lines, new)

---

## What shipped

Near-verbatim port of `~/Documents/systemcicy/INTERFACE.md` (229 lines). All thirteen of
its numbered sections stand, in order, with their original prose kept intact except at the
specific points below. Two required additions and the carried nine-states enumeration are
in place.

**Opening.** Rewrote the intro to state explicitly that this file is entirely the
tool-shaped half of the fork (`TRANSLATE.md` row 1), and to send page-shaped readers to
`STYLES.md` and `CRAFT.md` before section 1 starts — satisfying the brief's "say so and
point page-shaped readers at STYLES.md." Both `page-shaped` and `tool-shaped` appear
(`scripts/check.sh` greps for both, case-insensitive) — 8 total occurrences across the
file, not just the opening.

**Section 4, "The nine states."** Enumerated exactly as the carried constraint from Task 5
names them: empty, loading, partial, error, permission denied, offline/degraded, stale,
conflict, bulk — same table shape, same wording as source, since source's own naming
already matched the constraint verbatim. `CRAFT.md` line 36-37 and line 459 both reference
"the nine data states (`TOOLS.md`)" without enumerating; this file is now that source of
truth.

**New subsection: "Desktop window states,"** placed directly under section 4 as a sibling
required-state-set (not one of the thirteen numbered sections, so the "thirteen sections
stand as written" constraint holds). Sourced from `docs/research/tablet-desktop-verified.md`
lines 112–133: main / key / inactive, with the quoted mechanism (key window renders window
controls in color, becomes key only on click or keyboard-requiring focus; inactive grays
the same controls) and the two concrete failures it prevents — treating "not frontmost" as
"not receiving input," and a custom title bar that never updates so an operator with
several windows open can't tell which one their next keystroke lands in. Also carries the
research doc's two build obligations (custom chrome must hand-implement the transitions;
window controls at the toolbar's leading edge, critical content never under them).

**Section 7, navigation.** Added the trunk test as a new paragraph after the existing
bullets, sourced from `docs/audit/competitor-small-skills.md` line 350 (attributed
"gstack's design-review" inline, matching the family's existing convention of naming an
external source inline — `STYLES.md` line 22 does the same for a systemcicy quote). Framed
as a checkable rule: cover everything but the nav, can you still answer what site, what
page, what sections, where you are — with the tool-shaped-specific stakes (pays for the gap
daily, not once).

**Section 12, design system.** Added the STYLES.md pointer the brief requires as its own
paragraph: "small and strict" constrains the token set, not the style; `STYLES.md`'s
picking procedure and style-under-density check apply here exactly as they do
page-shaped; the plainest possible system is a choice in `STYLES.md`'s vocabulary, not the
default a tool is owed. This is the one clause systemcicy's INTERFACE.md structurally
cannot state, since systemcicy has no style catalog to point to — it assumes a plain
system throughout. Neither portfolio.me nor webcrab has the tool-shaped method to attach a
style pointer to. Only this merge can write this sentence.

**Section 13**, retitled "The deliverable" (was "Write `INTERFACE.md`, the Gate C
deliverable"). See mapping notes below for why.

---

## The §-renumbering map

Every bare `§N` in the source was checked against `~/Documents/systemcicy/PRINCIPLES.md`
(read in full to recover what each systemcicy number actually means — systemcicy's own
principles doc is not in this repo, so I could not skip this step) and then against
`PRINCIPLES.md` here for the matching concept. Three references had no home in this
repo's 16 principles and were dropped rather than forced (methodology: `STYLES.md`/
`CRAFT.md` already dropped one over-scoped `§9` citation on a similar judgment call, per
`progress.md` Task 4's note — the same call, made the same way).

| Source line | systemcicy `§` | systemcicy's own rule (from its `PRINCIPLES.md`) | This repo's `§` | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | `§5` | "The architecture is boring on purpose" (buys budget) | `§11` | Our `PRINCIPLES.md` has no architecture principle (no runtime in this plugin). `§11` "Performance is a design constraint, in two tiers" is the only principle here that names a "budget" by that word and follows the identical shape: restraint in one place funds attention in another. |
| 5 | `§6` | "The interface is not boring... See `INTERFACE.md`" (spends it here) | `§15` | `§15` is the principle that names `TOOLS.md` by name as where its detail lives ("The full state and shortcut set lives in `TOOLS.md`") — the exact structural role systemcicy's `§6` plays for `INTERFACE.md`. |
| 39, 78 | `§9` | "Every state is designed. Nine of them..." | *(dropped)* | Our `§9` is "Anti-slop, aimed at what the images say" — unrelated. The nine states have no `PRINCIPLES.md` home in this repo by design: per the carried constraint, `TOOLS.md` itself is the source of truth, referenced by name from `CRAFT.md`, not by number. Citations replaced with "(below)" (line 39) or dropped from the header (line 78, self-referential). |
| 57 | `§14` | "Accessible and keyboard-complete [HARD]" | `§15` | This repo splits systemcicy's combined accessibility+keyboard rule into `§10` (general accessibility) and `§15` (keyboard completeness specifically, `[HARD for tool-shaped surfaces]`). The section is titled "Keyboard completeness," so `§15` is the match. |
| 87, 155, 221 | `§25` | "The system's own words are written, not generated" | *(dropped)* | No copy/UX-writing principle exists in this repo's 16. `§9` (anti-slop) was already established in Task 4 as scoped narrowly to *image-generated* text, not general UI copy (`progress.md` Task 4 note) — forcing it here would repeat that exact overreach. Dropped in all three places (the `Error` state row, the section 9 header, and the deliverable list item 8); the prose stands unaided in each case. |
| 142 | `§7` | "Authorization is proven by a test on every path [HARD]" | *(dropped)* | No authorization/security principle exists in this repo — inter.face has no backend or runtime to enforce anything server-side. This is not one of the brief's three named file-qualified reaches (it's a bare `§`, not `ARCHITECTURE.md §7`), so it fell to the same case-by-case judgment as the `§25` instances. The guidance itself ("hiding is in addition to the [check], never instead of it") is still valid, generic advice for whoever builds the eventual tool, so it stayed; only the numeral was cut. |
| 182 | `§15` | "Performance is a workflow constraint. Measure the operator's task" | `§11` | Direct concept match to this repo's performance principle. |
| 204 | `§14` | (same combined rule as above) "Nothing conveyed by color alone" | `§10` | The "color alone" clause sits inside systemcicy's combined accessibility+keyboard `§14`. In this repo that clause's substance belongs with `§10` (general accessibility, `[HARD]`, covers contrast) rather than `§15` (keyboard specifically) — `§10` doesn't spell out "never color alone" verbatim, but it's the accessibility umbrella rule and the natural home for a WCAG-style non-text-contrast rule. Flagged here as the one citation broadened slightly rather than found verbatim, same category of call as the Task 5 icon-grade note. |

**Gate names**, not `§` but the same renumbering problem: systemcicy's `INTERFACE.md` cites
its own pipeline's Gate C (experience) and Gate D (per-slice), and its "Skip cost" section
says "the experience loop" — systemcicy's `loops/03-experience.md`, confirmed by listing
`~/Documents/systemcicy/loops/`. This repo has exactly two gates (`§16`: Gate A direction,
Gate B craft; "no B1/B2 leakage" per `progress.md` Task 5 note, and the plan confirms no
Gate C/D exist here). Line 33's "At Gate C and at every Gate D" became "At Gate A, and
again at Gate B." The "Skip cost" section's "the experience loop" became a description of
what's actually being skipped (designing the day, not a named loop that doesn't exist
here). Section 13's "The Gate C deliverable" for a per-run `INTERFACE.md` file became "For
a tool-shaped surface, `DIRECTION.md` carries these... decided across Gate A and Gate B" —
in this repo the per-run deliverable is `DIRECTION.md`, not a second file named after this
one; systemcicy uses the same filename for both its reference doc and its per-run output,
which this repo's file-naming scheme doesn't support (`TOOLS.md` is the reference; there is
no per-run `TOOLS.md`).

---

## How the three cut doc-refs were handled

All three are file-qualified reaches the brief named explicitly. In each case the
sentence's substance was already present without the citation, so the citation was simply
removed — nothing needed inlining because nothing outside the sentence was load-bearing:

1. **`DOMAIN.md §2`** (line 158, "using the client's nouns from `DOMAIN.md §2`") — this
   repo has no domain-modeling file (`TRANSLATE.md`'s six rows were checked; none covers
   "the client's own vocabulary" as a distinct concept). Reworded to "using the operator's
   own nouns for their own concepts" — same instruction, no dangling file reference.
2. **`ARCHITECTURE.md §7`** (line 153, background operations with progress/notification,
   "not a frozen screen") — the substance is the sentence itself; nothing further to
   inline. Citation dropped, sentence otherwise unchanged.
3. **`ARCHITECTURE.md §9`** (line 177, offline behavior "decided at Gate B: what queues,
   what does not, what the conflict state is") — same treatment. "Gate B" itself was kept
   since Gate B is a real, existing gate in this repo's model (`§16`); only the
   file-qualified citation was cut.

No dangling reference to a file that doesn't exist in this repo remains (`grep -n
'DOMAIN.md\|ARCHITECTURE.md\|Gate C\|Gate D' TOOLS.md` returns nothing).

---

## Check output

Baseline before this task: 12 `FAIL:` lines (per Task 5's report, after `CRAFT.md` cleared
its own fork-check failure). After this task: still 12 `FAIL:` lines, but `TOOLS.md`'s
fork-check line flips from `FAIL: TOOLS.md missing` to `ok: TOOLS.md forks on surface
class` — one failure cleared, replaced by nothing new, net count held steady only because
the count itself already excludes the file that just started passing.

```

  ok: no placeholders
== resident budget ==
  FAIL: AGENTS.md missing
== json validity ==
  FAIL: .claude-plugin/plugin.json missing
  FAIL: .claude-plugin/marketplace.json missing
  FAIL: .codex-plugin/plugin.json missing
  FAIL: gemini-extension.json missing
  FAIL: opencode.json missing
== skill frontmatter ==
  FAIL: skills/inter.face/SKILL.md missing
  FAIL: commands/interface.md missing
  FAIL: .cursor/rules/inter.face.mdc missing
== internal links resolve ==
  ok: all relative links resolve
== every reference file forks on surface class ==
  ok: STYLES.md forks on surface class
  ok: CRAFT.md forks on surface class
  ok: TOOLS.md forks on surface class          <-- new, was "FAIL: TOOLS.md missing"
  FAIL: SURFACES.md missing
  FAIL: ACCESS.md missing
== Apple numbers ship as pairs ==
  FAIL: SURFACES.md missing

CHECKS FAILED
```

All 12 remaining failures are the expected baseline for files Tasks 7+ create
(`AGENTS.md`, five plugin manifests, three adapter files, `SURFACES.md`, `ACCESS.md`). No
new failures. No placeholder hits (`example.com`, `TBD`, `TODO`, `Lorem ipsum`, `test
claim`, `FIXME`, `XXX` — all clear). No markdown links anywhere in the file (`grep -nE
'\]\(' TOOLS.md` returns nothing) — `STYLES.md`, `CRAFT.md`, `TRANSLATE.md`,
`PRINCIPLES.md`, `DIRECTION.md`, `loops/02-craft.md` all appear in backticks and prose
only.

---

## Concerns for the next tasks

1. **Three `§` citations were dropped rather than renumbered** (`§9`/nine-states, `§25`/
   copy, `§7`/authorization) because this repo's 16-rule `PRINCIPLES.md` has no matching
   concept for any of the three. This is a wider gap than the brief's "exactly three
   reaches" framing anticipated — those three were file-qualified reaches into
   `DOMAIN.md`/`ARCHITECTURE.md`; these are bare-`§` reaches into systemcicy's own
   `PRINCIPLES.md` numbers that this repo's `PRINCIPLES.md` never adopted. Judgment calls,
   not fabricated numbers. Flagging per the project's own "minor (deferred)" convention
   rather than silently forcing a bad fit.
2. **`§10` for "never color alone"** is the one citation broadened rather than matched
   verbatim — our `§10` doesn't spell out the color-alone rule in its own text, only
   general accessibility + contrast. Same category as Task 5's icon-grade citation note.
3. **Section 13's reframing is the largest structural change in the port.** Systemcicy
   uses the filename `INTERFACE.md` for both its reference doc and each run's own
   deliverable; this repo's naming scheme has no second `TOOLS.md`, so the per-run
   deliverable was mapped to `DIRECTION.md` instead, gated across Gate A and Gate B rather
   than a nonexistent Gate C. `loops/01-direction.md` and `loops/02-craft.md` don't exist
   yet (Task 10) — when they're written, confirm they actually route tool-shaped
   `DIRECTION.md` content the way this section now claims.

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)

3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

113	
114	> A macOS window can have one of three states: **Main** … **Key** … **Inactive**.
115	
116	The key window is the one receiving keyboard input, and it *"uses color in the title bar
117	options for closing, minimizing, and zooming; inactive windows and main windows that aren't
118	key use gray."* A window becomes key only when someone clicks its title bar or a component
119	requiring keyboard input.

121	Design obligations that have no web equivalent:
122

## Fix round 1 — review finding, Important

**Commit:** `f2bbf44b7d73f4196b6c6506bae98383b1c62c07`

Review approved everything except one Important finding: the **Main** row of the desktop
window states table contradicted its own source. It read "The window someone is working
in. Content and controls read as fully live." But
`docs/research/tablet-desktop-verified.md:116-118` quotes Apple directly: the key window
"uses color in the title bar options for closing, minimizing, and zooming; **inactive
windows and main windows that aren't key use gray**." A window that is Main but not Key —
a document window with a floating inspector or Find panel holding key focus, the ordinary
case where the two diverge — renders gray, not "fully live." Only the Main row had this
problem; Key and Inactive already matched the quote correctly, so the three rows
contradicted each other as a set.

**Fix.** Re-read `docs/research/tablet-desktop-verified.md` lines 112–133 in full before
touching anything, per the standing sourcing rule (nothing ships unless it traces to
verified research). The passage defines Main only by contrast with Key — "one of three
states," and the quoted quality ("main windows that aren't key use gray") — it does not
independently define what Main means (the source's own blockquote at line 114 elides
Main's definition with an ellipsis: "Main … Key … Inactive"). So the row was rewritten to
assert only what the passage supports — Main is a state distinct from Key; color renders
only when Main is also Key; Main-without-Key grays exactly like Inactive — rather than
adding an unsourced definition of Main (e.g. "frontmost window for the app"), which the
passage doesn't state. New wording:

> **Main** | Distinct from Key. Controls render in color only when this window is also Key
> — the common case. When Main but not Key, controls gray, the same rendering as Inactive
> | Assuming Main alone means colored, "live" chrome — a document window that stays Main
> while a floating inspector or Find panel holds Key still renders gray, and coloring
> every Main window regardless of Key ships backwards from what macOS actually shows

The document-window-plus-inspector scenario in "The failure" column is an illustrative
example, not a claim attributed to the source — same device the rest of the file already
uses throughout (the queue-and-technician day in section 1, the credit-limit error in
section 9). No new factual claim about macOS beyond what's quoted at lines 116–118 was
added. Key and Inactive rows were left untouched; they already read correctly.

**Check.** `./scripts/check.sh` re-run after the fix: same 12 `FAIL:` lines as before this
round, all the same expected missing-file baseline. `TOOLS.md` still shows `ok: TOOLS.md
forks on surface class`. No regression.
